incidents.incident: Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist (Lazarus Group), 4-5 February 2016
incidents.narrative_before: From 2014 Lazarus operators spear-phished Bangladesh Bank staff with fake job-applicant emails; recipients downloaded the payload, and the attackers then 'moved through the bank's network' to the computers used to send and receive SWIFT messages (DOJ complaint via PYMNTS). The bank's SWIFT room (four servers, eighth floor annex) sat on the same flat network as ~5,000 staff PCs, joined by unmanaged $10 switches with no firewall (Reuters/Daily Star). On 4-5 Feb 2016, over the Bangladeshi weekend, 35 fraudulent SWIFT instructions totalling about $951m were sent to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; $81m reached Philippine accounts and a $20m Sri Lanka transfer was stopped, the rest blocked after a 'fandation' typo (CSO, PYMNTS). Custom malware (evtdiag.exe) registered as a service in the SWIFT Alliance Access environment, patched a validity check with a two-byte change, deleted records of outgoing transfers in the Oracle DB and suppressed the confirmation printer, delaying discovery (BAE, CSO, Threatpost). Defenders first noticed an empty printer on Friday 5 Feb and treated it as a routine fault; only on Saturday 6 Feb, after the SWIFT terminal failed with 'A file is missing or changed' and was restarted by 12:30, did manual printing (24h later) reveal 46 Fed queries about the payments (Bloomberg/FA-mag).

ambiguities: The specific lateral tooling between the phished workstation and the SWIFT server is not described in public sources (BAE: 'unknown how the malware was loaded onto the network'); the single link pc_phish->srv_swift_alliance reflects the DOJ complaint's statement that the actors 'moved through the bank's network'.
No public source names a domain controller, file server or use of domain credentials, so no dc/files machines or workstation->dc links were added.

The SWIFT room held four servers (Reuters); only the Alliance Access host is described. The other three are included with plain defaults and unspecified roles; whether they were compromised is not stated, so they are not in the hacked set.
The '~5,000 computers' is a generic group; three representative workstations plus the phished one are modelled.
The confirmation printer is treated as a function of srv_swift_alliance (printing via nroff.exe on the Alliance host), not as a separate machine.

Leftover risk on srv_swift_alliance set to 7 (monitoring/C2 server in Egypt, BAE via CSO). The attackers also impersonated authorised SWIFT operators (DOJ), but no source states domain-admin credential theft, so 8 was not applied. pc_phish set to 5 (initial access confirmed; no post-exploitation artefact on that host is described).

The exact fetch of the full BAE technical blog (baesystemsai.blogspot.co.uk/2016/04/two-bytes-to-951m.html) was blocked; the liboradb.dll detail of the two-byte patch is therefore not cited, only the 'two bytes' claim as reported by CSO.
Oracle DB is described as part of the Alliance Access environment on the same host; it was not split into a separate machine or depends_on entry.

Saturday 6 Feb 2016: SWIFT terminal software 'wasn't responding'; restart shows 'A file is missing or changed'; terminal back by 12:30; after >24h of manual printing the receipts show the New York Fed had sent queries against 46 payment orders. Real detection of the fraud.

incidents.incident: WannaCry ransomware on NHS England (modelled as one representative infected acute trust), 12 May 2017
incidents.narrative_before: On Friday 12 May 2017 the WannaCry worm, attributed by the UK to North Korea's Lazarus group (NCSC), hit the NHS: at least 80 of 236 trusts in England were affected - 34 infected and locked out of devices (25 acute) and 46 reporting disruption - plus 603 primary-care and other organisations including 595 GP practices (NAO HC 414 paras 1.2, 5). It spread 'via the internet, including through the N3 network' and 'exploited weaknesses within parts of Microsoft's Windows operating system used to share files within organisations' (SMBv1, MS17-010, patch issued 14 March 2017 - NAO paras 1.2, 2.9; CISA TA17-181A); most infected devices were unpatched but supported Windows 7, and managing internet-facing firewalls would have blocked infection regardless of patching (NAO paras 2.4-2.5). Trusts first reported problems late morning; NHS England's EPRR team was notified at 13:06, declared a major incident at 16:00, took the lead at 18:45, and a researcher's kill-switch domain stopped new infections that evening (NAO Figure 2, para 1). 6,912 appointments were confirmed cancelled (19,494 estimated), five acute trusts diverted ambulances, and by 19 May 1,220 diagnostic devices (~1% of such equipment, including MRI scanners) were identified as infected, with radiology and pathology disrupted (NAO paras 1.3, 1.7, 1.8). DHSC later estimated the cost at £92m (£20m lost output, £72m IT restoration); no ransom was paid and no patient data was stolen (DHSC via NHE; NAO).

ambiguities: The NAO report describes the attack at national/aggregate level; it does not name any individual trust's hosts. The machine set is a representative single acute trust built from the report's host classes (unpatched Windows 7 devices, MRI scanners on embedded XP, other diagnostic devices). Counts per class are the brief's generic-group allowance, not reported figures.

Which specific trust was first infected and the exact first host are not public; web_smb_entry represents the NAO's statement that managing internet-facing firewalls would have prevented infection (para 2.4).

The NAO does not state that any infected device was in life-critical use and could not be disconnected; it says trusts themselves shut down or isolated devices (para 1.4). isolatable therefore stays true for all devices.
No source mentions domain controllers, file servers or domain credentials (WannaCry does not use credentials), so no dc/files machines or workstation->dc links were added.

Services: the NAO reports disruption to A&E (ambulance diverts), appointments, radiology and pathology but names no servers (PAS, RIS, LIMS). Workstation replicas for A&E and appointments stand in for 'locked out of devices' (para 1.2); this is a modelling choice, logged here.
Exact spread pattern (which host infected which) is not reported; links form a plausible star/tree consistent with 'spread automatically' via SMB, one link per hop in the modelled path.
Kill-switch time: NAO says 'on the evening of 12 May' (para 1) without a clock time.
DHSC figures: NHE reports £20m/£72m split; some outlets quote £19m/£73m. The NHE values are used.
The NAO web summary states 'at least 81 of 236 trusts'; the full report says 'at least 80' (34 locked out + 46 disrupted), after three trusts were recategorised. The full-report figure is used.

incidents.incident: NotPetya wiper at A.P. Moller-Maersk, 27 June 2017 (Sandworm / M.E.Doc supply-chain)
incidents.narrative_before: In spring 2017 Sandworm backdoored the update servers of Linkos Group's Ukrainian tax software M.E.Doc (dev environment compromised from 14 April per CISA TA17-181A); on 27 June the poisoned update ran NotPetya via the EzVit.exe updater (Microsoft). At Maersk the only foothold was a single computer in the Odessa office on which a Ukraine finance executive had asked IT to install M.E.Doc (Wired). The worm spread with EternalBlue/EternalRomance SMBv1 exploits (CVE-2017-0144/0145, MS17-010) and a Mimikatz-style credential dumper feeding PsExec and WMIC, scanning entire subnets when it landed on a server or domain controller (Microsoft, CISA); within hours it had wiped essentially all of Maersk's ~150 domain controllers, 4,000 servers and 45,000 PCs (Wired). Defenders first saw it in Copenhagen that afternoon when an IT administrator's PC spontaneously rebooted and 'a wave of screens turning black' swept the open-plan office; disconnecting the global network took more than two hours (Wired). Maerskline.com booking went down and the APM Terminals gate at Elizabeth, NJ went dead, backing trucks up for miles; the only intact domain-controller copy was recovered from an office in Ghana that had been offline in a blackout, and core infrastructure was rebuilt in about 10 days from a Maidenhead emergency centre, with port operations normalising over ~2 weeks (Wired, Control Engineering). Maersk booked a USD 200-300m hit, mainly at Maersk Line, APM Terminals and Damco (CNBC, Q2 2017 interim report).

ambiguities: No public source gives Maersk's internal host-to-host path. Links follow the propagation mechanism described by Microsoft/CISA (credential theft -> PsExec/WMIC/SMB; DCs and servers scanning multiple subnets) and the outcomes reported by Wired (all DCs, Copenhagen PCs, booking site, NJ gate). The specific link pc_odessa_medoc->dc is inferred from Mimikatz credential use + 'all domain controllers wiped'; which DC was hit first is unknown.

~150 domain controllers are collapsed into a single 'dc' machine plus 'dc_ghana' (the only surviving copy). dc_ghana was offline and never infected; the dc->dc_ghana link reflects normal AD replication and the fact that only its outage saved it.
'45,000 PCs' and '4,000 servers' are generic groups; 5 Copenhagen PCs and 4 generic servers are modelled. Wired gives 45,000 PCs; some secondary sources say 49,000 laptops - the Wired figure is used.

Leftover risk on dc at m1 set to 8 (credential theft, T1003) because the sources do not state whether the DCs were already wiped at the moment the Copenhagen screens went black; at m2 set to 9 (wiped, T1485). All other hacked hosts set to 9 (wiper deployed) since NotPetya encrypts/overwrites immediately on execution.

Whether the Elizabeth gate system and Maerskline.com depend on Active Directory is not stated; depends_on dc is a modelling assumption consistent with Wired's account that AD loss was the root blocker to recovery.
Services for Maersk Line vessel operations, Damco, and other APM terminals (76 ports) are not modelled separately because the sources give no system-level detail for them.
Cost: Maersk's own Q2 2017 statement says USD 200-300m (CNBC); Wired/Snabe quote $250-300m. Both are cited.
No 'files' file server is named in any source; workstation->dc links were added because domain credentials (Mimikatz) were used.

incidents.incident: Norsk Hydro - LockerGoga ransomware (detected night of 18-19 March 2019)
incidents.narrative_before: In December 2018 a Hydro employee opened an email attachment sent by an employee of a trusted customer as part of an apparently legitimate conversation; it installed a Trojan, which antivirus flagged a few days later, but 'by then, the attacker had built an initial foothold' (Microsoft DART case study). Over the following months the attacker compromised standard user accounts, then captured administrative credentials and, in the night of 18-19 March 2019, deployed LockerGoga 'via a manual push from Hydro's own domain controllers' (Microsoft); NorCERT confirmed 'the attack was combined with an attack on Active Directory' (BankInfoSecurity). At about 4 a.m. an IT colleague phoned Hydro's information security officer: 'We may be under attack'; production had already stopped at some of the 170 plants and IT shut down the network and servers to stop the spread (Microsoft). Files on thousands of servers and PCs were locked across 35,000 employees in 40 countries; Extruded Solutions suffered the most, while Bauxite & Alumina, Primary Metal, Rolled Products and Energy continued on manual procedures (Hydro.com). Hydro refused to pay, rebuilt encrypted machines from backups, estimated the Q1 2019 cost at NOK 300-450 million (USD 35-52m) with a further NOK 200-250m in Q2, and the total approached USD 71 million (Reuters/SecurityWeek/Microsoft).

incidents.incident: Universitaetsklinikum Duesseldorf (UKD) - DoppelPaymer ransomware via Citrix CVE-2019-19781 (10 September 2020)
incidents.narrative_before: Attackers exploited CVE-2019-19781 ('Shitrix') in the hospital's Citrix Gateway/ADC VPN appliance between its disclosure on 17 December 2019 and the January 2020 patch, and planted a loader on an internal clinic server that survived the patch and two external re-checks (NRW Justice Ministry via dpa; BSI: attackers 'kept access even after the fix'). In the night of 10-11 September 2020 the loader pulled DoppelPaymer and encrypted 30 clinic servers; the hospital's IT failed on Thursday 10 September, the UKD deregistered from emergency care and postponed planned and outpatient treatment, and e-mail was still down on 14 September (Landtag statement, UKD updates via Borncity). An extortion note addressed to the Heinrich-Heine-Universitaet was found on one server; after Duesseldorf police told the attackers they had hit a hospital, they sent the decryption key (Computerwoche/dpa). In the night of 11-12 September a patient with an aortic tear was diverted to Wuppertal, treated about an hour later than planned, and died; the prosecutor dropped the negligent-homicide inquiry in November 2020 because 'the delay had no bearing on the final outcome' (Wired via Borncity). The central emergency department was expected to reopen only in the week of 21-25 September (dpa).

incidents.incident: Colonial Pipeline - DarkSide ransomware (intrusion 29 April, ransom note 7 May 2021)
incidents.narrative_before: DarkSide affiliates logged into Colonial Pipeline's network on 29 April 2021 through a legacy VPN profile 'that was not intended to be in use', which had only single-factor authentication and whose complex password later turned up in a dark-web batch of leaked credentials (Blount testimony; Mandiant via Bloomberg). On Thursday 6 May they exfiltrated about 100 GB of data from the IT network in roughly two hours and then encrypted computers (Bloomberg). Just before 5:00 AM EDT on Friday 7 May an employee found the ransom note on a system in the IT network; the Control Center operations supervisor ordered a stop-work and by 6:10 AM all 5,500 miles of pipeline were shut down to keep the malware from reaching the OT network, which Mandiant later confirmed the attackers never entered (Blount; CISA AA21-131A; Carmakal). Colonial paid about USD 4.4 million (75 BTC) on 8 May, of which DOJ later seized 63.7 BTC, and restarted the pipeline on the evening of 12 May; fuel shortages hit 13 states and D.C. served from 29 Gulf Coast refineries, and seven finance systems were only restored on 8 June (Blount; Dark Reading).

incidents.incident: Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) — Conti ransomware (Wizard Spider), 14 May 2021
incidents.narrative_before: On 16 March 2021 a phishing email with a malicious Excel attachment was sent to an HSE user; it was opened on 18 March on the 'Patient Zero Workstation' and the attacker achieved persistence by 23 March (PwC pp. 2, 28). On 31 March the HSE antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on that workstation but 'was set to monitor mode so it did not block the malicious commands' and no incident was raised (PwC p. 29). On 7 May the attacker 'conducted AD and domain reconnaissance, and compromised further systems within the HSE' and 'was identified as using highly privileged accounts for the first time'; antivirus flagged Cobalt Strike on six HSE servers that day and the alerts were not actioned (PwC p. 29; HHS). Between 8 and 12 May six voluntary hospitals and one statutory hospital were compromised; Hospital C found malicious activity on a domain controller on 10 May, Hospital A alerted the HSE on 12 May and reset 4,500 passwords, and on 13 May the AV vendor emailed about 'unhandled threat events since 7 May 2021 on at least 16 systems' — the HSE response was to ask the server team to restart servers (PwC pp. 28-30). At 01:00 on 14 May Conti was executed; hospitals reported encrypted systems at 02:50, encryption in the HSE data centre was identified at 04:36, and the HSE shut down all IT and the National Healthcare Network. About 80% of the environment was encrypted and ~700 GB exfiltrated; NIMIS radiology, laboratory, radiotherapy, maternity (MN-CMS) and iPMS systems were lost, ~7,000 appointments a day were cancelled, a decryption key appeared on 20 May, full server decryption took until September 2021 and the HSE put the cost at >= EUR 100m (PwC pp. 15, 32-33; HHS; Irish Times).

incidents.incident: Change Healthcare (UnitedHealth Group / Optum) — ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware, 21 February 2024
incidents.narrative_before: On 12 February 2024 'criminals used compromised credentials to remotely access a Change Healthcare Citrix portal, an application used to enable remote access to desktops. The portal did not have multi-factor authentication' (Witty, Senate Finance testimony). Over the next nine days the attackers 'moved laterally within the systems in more sophisticated ways and exfiltrated data'; because Change's prime and backup environments were not isolated, the backups were encrypted too, which Witty called 'really the root cause' of the long recovery (Cybersecurity Dive). On 21 February 2024 ALPHV/BlackCat deployed ransomware 'encrypting Change's systems so we could not access them'; the same day UnitedHealth 'identified a suspected nation-state associated cyber security threat actor' and 'proactively isolated the impacted systems', severing Change's data-centre connections so that malware did not spread beyond Change (8-K; testimony). Pharmacy claims, medical claims and payment processing for much of the US stopped: 99% of pre-incident pharmacies were only back by 7 March, payments were at ~86% of pre-incident levels at the time of the hearing, and UHG had advanced more than $6.5bn to providers (testimony). UHG confirmed on 29 February the actor was ALPHV/BlackCat, paid a ransom (an affiliate cited a $22m Bitcoin transaction), booked $872m of Q1 2024 costs, and ultimately notified ~190 million people (TechCrunch; TechTarget).

sources.what_it_gave: entry point (12 Feb, compromised credentials, Citrix remote-access portal, no MFA), lateral movement + exfiltration, ransomware deployed nine days later, data centre connections severed, ransom decision, rebuild (laptops replaced, credentials rotated, data centre network and core services rebuilt), restoration figures (pharmacy 99% by 7 March, payments ~86%, $6.5bn advanced)

ambiguities: Public sources never name individual internal hosts; srv_core_1..3, pc_desktop_1..3 and pc_laptop_1..3 are generic placeholders for 'Change Healthcare's data center network and core services', the Citrix-published desktops and the 'thousands of laptops' replaced (rule 1, 3-10 per generic group).

No Active Directory / domain controller is named in testimony or filings; 'rotated credentials' implies domain credentials were at risk but no source says domain credentials were used for lateral movement, so no 'dc' machine and no workstation -> dc links were added.

The order of lateral hops between the desktop, core servers, claims platforms and backups is not public; the links fan out from a single srv_core_1 pivot as the simplest structure consistent with 'moved laterally ... in more sophisticated ways' and 'travel freely between servers' (Nebraska complaint via TechCrunch).

srv_backup is modelled as a single shared replica for all three core services; which services the backups covered is not stated. Replicas = 2 only because Witty explicitly said backup systems existed (and were encrypted).
Exfiltration method/staging host is not public (ALPHV commonly uses rclone/Mega per AA23-353A); no exfil host added.
The $22m ransom figure is an ALPHV affiliate's claim about a Bitcoin transaction (TechCrunch); UHG confirmed paying but never stated the amount.
190 million affected (Jan 2025) comes from UHG's updated HHS breach notice, not from the May 2024 testimony, which said 'about one third' of Americans.

Only one detection moment exists: the 8-K and testimony place discovery on 21 Feb, coincident with ransomware deployment; hence encrypted hosts carry T1486 risk 9 at that moment. Hosts are limited to Change's own environment ('contained the blast radius to just Change').
CISA AA23-353A could not be fetched in this session; it is cited only as the ALPHV technique reference.

Eligibility and other Change products were disrupted according to press reports but are not itemised in the testimony retrieved, so only pharmacy claims, medical claims and payments are modelled as services.

moments.description: 21 February 2024: first and only defender detection — ransomware is deployed inside Change's IT environment and UHG identifies the intrusion the same day, isolating Change's data centres from the rest of UHG. Nine days of undetected access (12-21 Feb) preceded it; no earlier alert is described in any public source. Citrix portal = initial access via valid credentials (5); desktop = lateral foothold (6); encrypted servers incl. backups = T1486 (9).
